segs.text: Module three, objective seven. The plasma concentration, C p, at any time during or after an infusion. While the infusion runs, drug comes in at a constant rate, R, and C p rises toward C s s, the steady state concentration. Once it stops, which is called cessation, nothing comes in and C p falls by first order elimination: a fixed fraction, k, is lost each hour. The level at the moment the infusion stops, C peak, joins the two phases: it is the end of the rise and the start of the fall.

card.m: C<sub>peak</sub>: the end of the rise, the start of the fall

segs.text: How high C peak is depends on how long the infusion ran, counted in half-lives. One half-life of infusion reaches half of C s s, two reach seventy five percent, and only after three to five half-lives is C peak close to C s s. After cessation the fraction lost each hour is k whatever the starting level, so on a log plot the fall has the same slope whether the infusion stopped at steady state or before it. A higher C peak loses more milligrams per liter each hour, but the same fraction.

card.m: infusion length 1 half-life → 50%; 2 → 75%; 3 to 5 → close to C<sub>ss</sub>
after cessation: same k, same slope, from any C<sub>peak</sub>
higher C<sub>peak</sub>: larger fall per hour, same fraction

segs.text: During the infusion, C p equals R over clearance, times one minus e to the minus k t, with t counted from the start of the infusion. Putting t equal to the infusion length gives C peak. After cessation, C p equals C peak times e to the minus k t, with t now counted from cessation. C peak plays the part of C zero, the starting concentration, in the I V bolus equation, and on a plot of the natural log of C p against time the fall is a straight line. She said, Think of that C peak as your C zero as your starting point.

card.m: during: C<sub>p</sub> = {{frac:R|Cl}}(1 − e<sup>−kt</sup>), t from the start
after: C<sub>p</sub> = C<sub>peak</sub>e<sup>−kt</sup>, t from cessation
C<sub>peak</sub> plays C<sub>0</sub>; ln C<sub>p</sub> against time: straight, slope −k

segs.text: After cessation, the key decision is C peak, the level the fall starts from. If the infusion ran to steady state, C peak is C s s; if it ran for a stated shorter time, C peak must first be computed from the rising equation. Two adjacent parts of one practice set often differ only in this, so the infusion length in each part decides the starting point. When a time is a whole number of half-lives, halves can be counted instead of evaluating the exponential, and she shows both routes.

card.m: ran to steady state: C<sub>peak</sub> = C<sub>ss</sub>

segs.text: Her slide Example six: one hundred fifty milligrams is infused over six hours, k is zero point two three one per hour, V D, the apparent volume of distribution, is fifteen liters, and the question asks C p three hours after cessation. The fall needs a starting point, so the first question is whether six hours reached steady state. The rate is twenty five milligrams per hour, the clearance three point four six five liters per hour, and C s s seven point two one five milligrams per liter. The half-life is three hours, so six hours of infusion is only two half-lives, which reach seventy five percent of C s s.

card.m: 150 mg over 6 hr; k = 0.231 hr<sup>−1</sup>; V<sub>D</sub> = 15 L
t<sub>½</sub> = {{frac:0.693|0.231 hr<sup>−1</sup>}} = 3 hr; 6 hr = 2 half-lives: not at steady state

segs.text: In her Example six, C peak is C s s, seven point two one five milligrams per liter, times the fraction reached at six hours: five point four one milligrams per liter, seventy five percent of C s s. Three hours after cessation is one more half-life, so the level halves to two point seven one milligrams per liter, her stated two point seven. Assuming steady state instead would start the fall at seven point two one five and give about three point six milligrams per liter, which is wrong because six hours is only two half-lives.

Her slide Example five starts from steady state: an infusion that reached fifteen milligrams per liter, a five hour half-life, and C p twelve hours after cessation. Here C peak is C s s, fifteen milligrams per liter, and k is zero point one three eight six per hour. Fifteen times e to the minus k times twelve is two point eight four milligrams per liter. In class she changed twelve hours to ten, exactly two half-lives, and took a quarter of fifteen, three point seven five milligrams per liter; that written answer belongs to ten hours, and for the twelve hours asked the answer is two point eight four.

card.m: C<sub>ss</sub> = 15 mg/L, t<sub>½</sub> = 5 hr; C<sub>p</sub> 12 hr after cessation = ?
C<sub>peak</sub> = C<sub>ss</sub> = 15 mg/L; k = {{frac:0.693|5 hr}} = 0.1386 hr<sup>−1</sup>

segs.text: How she tests it: her stems give a number of hours after the cessation of the infusion and say whether a loading dose was given. In her review an infusion aimed at twenty four milligrams per liter stopped after five hours, with a five hour half-life. A student started the fall from eighteen milligrams per liter; one half-life of infusion reaches fifty percent of C s s, not seventy five, so C peak is twelve milligrams per liter, and three hours later the level is seven point nine milligrams per liter. The two equations count time differently: t in the rising one counts from the start, and t in the falling one counts from cessation.

card.m: C<sub>ss</sub> = 24 mg/L; stopped at 5 hr; k = 0.1386 hr<sup>−1</sup>
rising: t from the start; falling: t from cessation

segs.text: Her later review chained one more case. A two hour infusion of fifty milligrams per hour, with a three hour half-life and a V D of eighteen liters, ends at four point four five milligrams per liter. A second, identical infusion starts six hours after the first began, and the question asks the level four hours after it stops, twelve hours from the start. The first infusion's level falls from the moment it ends, at two hours. The second climbs exactly as the first did, on top of what is left of the first. At twelve hours the first has been falling for ten hours and the second for four, and the two levels add; her answer was two point two milligrams per liter.

card.m: her 10/19 review: 50 mg/hr for 2 hr, t<sub>½</sub> 3 hr, V<sub>D</sub> 18 L
k = {{frac:0.693|3 hr}} = 0.231 hr<sup>−1</sup>; C<sub>ss</sub> = {{frac:50 mg/hr|0.231 hr<sup>−1</sup> × 18 L}} = 12.02 mg/L
end of infusion: 12.02 mg/L × (1 − e−0.231 × 2) = 4.45 mg/L
second infusion 6 to 8 hr; read at 12 hr, 4 hr after it stops
first: 4.45 mg/L at 2 hr, then falls
